data.title: Starý plášť – a Bronze Age hillfort above Plavecký Mikuláš
data.excerpt: Starý plášť above Plavecký Mikuláš is a little-known but very fine Lesser Carpathian hillfort, lying at over 640 m in the limestone of the Plavecký karst. Rock faces up to 15 m high and a timber-and-earth rampart some 260 m long enclose an oval area of 1.9 ha, built and occupied by the people of the Velatice and later the Podolí culture.

children.text: little-known but very fine Lesser Carpathian hillfort is Starý plášť, which lies in the cadastral area of the village of Plavecký Mikuláš. Its name sounds rather mysterious, but a few months ago, on the forum of our

I came across a post in which a reader from the area around the hillfort stated that the original name was Stará plošť. Given the fairly level plateau of the hillfort, such a name would already make quite different sense. So far, however, I have not managed to trace this name on any old map, so we still have to treat this information with reserve. It can be approached both from the Orešany side and from Záhorie, since from both directions a waymarked path will bring you comfortably to Mon Repos, and from there you pass without difficulty through the stone gate onto the forest road leading to the hillfort.

This part of the mountain massif is formed of limestone making up the so-called „Plavecký karst“. Within the Lesser Carpathians the hillfort lies at a higher elevation, its altitude exceeding 640 m, and since the hillfort itself stands partly on a raised rock that protrudes from the forest cover, it is clearly visible from the surrounding country over a great distance. That at the same time means that the inhabitants of the hillfort had a very good view over a wide area, which is a great tactical advantage. On the western, southern and eastern sides the hillfort is protected by vertical rock faces up to 15 m high or by a steep slope. On the northern, most accessible side its defenders built a timber-and-earth rampart, the remains of which are in some parts still clearly visible. The rock faces, the steep slope and the fortification enclose an area of roughly oval shape measuring 190 × 140 m, with a total interior area of 1.9 ha, which is fairly level, although of course it is no ideal plain and there are places here with more pronounced differences in height.

children.text: As regards the description of the rampart defences, Juraj Bartík states that „the only element of the artificial fortification of Starý plášť known at present is the rampart protecting the approach from the north and the west. An arc that is readily observable in the field, heaped up from local limestone boulders whose largest dimensions exceed 0.5 m, though mostly they are only 0.2–0.3 m, runs for a length of approximately 180 m. In the west the rampart gradually fades from the human eye. In this part, however, its course is readily observable on a visualisation of the digital terrain model. The arc of the artificial fortification linking the north-eastern and the south-western edge of the rock face thus reaches a total length of around 260 m. In the northern, most massive part the collapse of stone and earth is 2 m high and up to 12 m wide. The present dimensions have, however, undoubtedly been altered by the slumping of the stone mass down the slope. No traces of a ditch showed in the field.“

In the north-eastern part of the rampart there is an entrance into the fortified enclosure that is still used today. It is evidently the original gateway, formed by the easternmost section of the rampart, which is curved towards the south. The „half-bastion“ protecting the eastern side of the entrance follows the natural configuration of the rocky subsoil, which was heightened by an artificial fortification. Both arms of the entrance are curved inwards into the hillfort and thus create a massive gateway with a funnel-shaped plan.

children.text: Despite the fact that the hillfort was discovered as early as the beginning of the 1950s, no trial archaeological excavation has been carried out on it to date, only surface collection. At the same time the hillfort has been looted by metal detectorists. Staff of the Slovak National Museum managed to document some of the illegally obtained finds. Two bronze socketed axes, together with a spectacle brooch, had been deposited together, just behind the rampart, to the east of the inner side of the entrance gateway. Spectacle brooches with a figure-of-eight loop occur above all in hoards of the Late and Final Urnfield period, and so the earliest dating of the hillfort can probably be assigned to this period as well.

A further documented assemblage of illegal finds from the hillfort consists of bronze knives of the Stillfried type, sickles and a fragment of a bracelet, which were not found in the interior of the Starý plášť hillfort but in its immediate vicinity, on the slope below the rampart and at the foot of the encircling rock face. They evidently did not form a coherent hoard; they are individual finds. In Slovakia they are at present represented above all at sites of the Lusatian culture, dated to the Final Bronze Age. The fragment of the bracelet is a piece of an open circular ornament with terminals slightly turned outwards. On the visible „outer“ side, this ornament for the wrist or the ankle was covered with decoration executed both by engraving and by punching (by punch impressions). Various local variants of this decoration cover bracelets and anklets in the Middle Danube region, in the eastern Alpine area and in Bohemia.

children.text: In the years 1993–2000 staff of the Slovak National Museum carried out surface collection at the site. They found numerous sherds of pottery vessels in the interior of the hillfort, above all in the area behind the northernmost section of the rampart. A fragment of the blade of a bronze knife was also found in this part. In the area of the western end of the rampart they found fragments of prehistoric pottery on the front side of the defences as well. Without exception the fragments are of small size and in the overwhelming majority undecorated. One of them, thick-walled, is heavily burnt secondarily. In no case was any graphite coating of the surface established.
The dating and occupation of the hillfort

On the basis of the pottery and of the bronze objects found, we can date the hillfort to the period of the Final Bronze Age, and its builders and inhabitants were evidently the people of the Velatice and later of the Podolí culture. In general this period belongs within the framework of the Urnfield people.

In his assessment of the hillfort, Juraj Bartík states that the Starý plášť hillfort did not lie in a region untouched by human activity, but in a landscape that was frequently visited and probably exploited economically. The mountain area was suited to the seasonal grazing of herd animals, to the gathering of forest fruits and to the hunting of game. The casting of bronze involved the consumption of charcoal, which in later periods was produced above all in wooded upland terrain. Archaeologically undocumented, but potentially possible, is prehistoric exploitation of ores in the area of copper mineralisation between Smolenice and Sološnica, that is to say in the immediate vicinity of the Starý plášť hillfort.
